name: Jewish communities
subtitle: of the Arab world & Iran
native_language: Judeo-Arabic, Ladino, Judeo-Farsi, Aramaic (Babylonian), Yemenite Hebrew
native_script: Hebrew/Aramaic square script; Judeo-Arabic in Hebrew letters
arabization_status: N/A — communities expelled before full Arabization; Hebrew maintained continuously
language_vitality: Endangered in diaspora; Judeo-Arabic and Ladino critically endangered
human_scale_fact: Jews had lived continuously in Babylon (Iraq) for 2,600 years — since the destruction of the First Temple in 586 BCE. They predate Islam in that land by over a millennium. Operation Magic Carpet (1949–50) airlifted 49,000 Yemenite Jews to Israel in 380 flights. Most had never seen an airplane.
key_quote: We did not leave. We were made to leave. There is a difference — and that difference matters to history.
key_quote_attribution: Shlomo Hillel, Iraqi-Jewish statesman and diplomat
israel_connection: Israel was founded in part as refuge for expelled Jewish communities. 850,000+ Jewish refugees from Arab lands resettled there — a displacement larger than the Palestinian refugee crisis, with no UN agency and no international compensation.

resources.label: Jewish Virtual Library — Jewish communities in Arab countries
JIMENA — Jews Indigenous to the Middle East and North Africa

name: Eastern Christian communities
subtitle: Coptic, Maronite, Greek Orthodox, Melkite
note_on_numbers: Absolute numbers grew (Copts especially) but share of MENA population collapsed from ~20% to ~4%.
native_language: Coptic (Egypt), Syriac/Aramaic (Iraq/Syria), Armenian, Greek, Arabic
native_script: Coptic alphabet (modified Greek), Syriac Estrangela script, Armenian script, Greek
arabization_status: Significant — Coptic language reduced to liturgy only; Syriac endangered; Greek Orthodox Arabized in language but not identity
language_vitality: Coptic: dormant (liturgical only). Syriac: endangered. Armenian: vulnerable.
human_scale_fact: Egypt's Coptic Church was founded by St. Mark in 42 CE — 600 years before Islam reached Egypt. Iraq's Christian population fell from 1.5 million in 2003 to under 200,000 today — an 87% collapse in 20 years driven not by one event but by sustained bombing, kidnapping, and murder.
key_quote: Our language is Aramaic — the language Jesus spoke. We have been here since before the caliphate, before the crusades, before Islam. We are not a remnant. We are the original people.
israel_connection: ~180,000 Arab Christians hold full Israeli citizenship. Nazareth — majority-Christian Arab city — is stable and growing. The only Arabic-speaking Christian community in the Middle East not in demographic freefall.

resources.label: Aid to the Church in Need — country reports

name: Assyrian & Syriac people
subtitle: an ethnic nation without a state
native_language: Neo-Aramaic (Assyrian, Chaldean, Turoyo dialects) — the closest living language to what Jesus spoke
native_script: Syriac script (Estrangela, Serto, East Syriac) — one of the oldest continuously used alphabets in the world
arabization_status: Severe — Assyrian place names Arabized; Syriac schools closed or restricted; Kurdish regions partially more tolerant
language_vitality: Endangered — estimated 500,000–800,000 speakers globally, majority in diaspora
human_scale_fact: The Assyrian language (Neo-Aramaic) is a direct descendant of the language spoken by Jesus of Nazareth. The Syriac script is older than the Arabic alphabet. The Nineveh Plains — site of the ancient Assyrian Empire capital — has been continuously inhabited for 7,000 years. It was emptied in 72 hours in August 2014.
key_quote: We are not refugees. We are indigenous. Nineveh is ours — not from yesterday, but from 7,000 years ago.
israel_connection: Small Assyrian community in Israel; Aramaic-speaking villages in Galilee (Jish/Gush Halav) maintain liturgical Aramaic.

name: Armenian people
subtitle: survivors of the first genocide of the 20th century
note_on_numbers: Survivors remaining in Turkey/region; global Armenian diaspora ~8 million worldwide; Republic of Armenia established 1991.
native_language: Armenian (Eastern and Western dialects)
native_script: Armenian alphabet — invented by Mesrop Mashtots in 405 CE; one of the most distinctive scripts in the world
arabization_status: Minimal — Armenians maintained script and language through diaspora institutions; Turkey attempted Turkification
language_vitality: Western Armenian (diaspora): endangered. Eastern Armenian (Republic of Armenia): healthy.
human_scale_fact: The Armenian Quarter of Jerusalem has been continuously inhabited since the 4th century CE — predating Islam, the Ottoman Empire, and modern Turkey. The Armenians were the first nation to adopt Christianity as a state religion (301 CE). Turkey officially denies the genocide that every major historian, the International Association of Genocide Scholars, and 32 countries recognize.
key_quote: They can kill us. They can exile us. They cannot kill our language. As long as one Armenian child reads our letters, we survive.
key_quote_attribution: Komitas Vardapet, Armenian composer and genocide survivor, 1915
israel_connection: Armenian Quarter in Jerusalem's Old City dates to 4th century CE. ~1,500 Armenians in Haifa; genocide survivors arrived in 1920s. Israel recognized Armenian Genocide in 2021.

resources.label: Zoryan Institute for Contemporary Armenian Research
Houshamadyan — reconstruction of Ottoman Armenian life

name: Yazidi people
subtitle: survivors of the 74th Ferman
native_language: Kurmanji Kurdish (primary); some speak Arabic
native_script: Modified Latin (Turkey/diaspora); Arabic script (Iraq); Kurdish Badini dialect
arabization_status: Significant in Iraq — Sinjar district Arabized under Saddam; place names changed; land redistributed to Arab tribes
language_vitality: Kurmanji Kurdish: vulnerable; oral Yazidi religious texts (Kitêba Cilwe, Mishefa Reş) transmitted orally for centuries — now being transcribed
human_scale_fact: August 3, 2014 is commemorated as Yazidi Genocide Day. In Yazidi oral history, this was the 74th Ferman — the 74th attempt to eliminate them. Yazidi theology holds that they cannot convert others and cannot marry outside the faith: each person killed or enslaved is irreplaceable. The largest Yazidi community outside Iraq is now in Hanover, Germany — an ancient Mesopotamian mountain faith now practicing in European cities.
key_quote: They came because we are different. They called us devil worshippers. We who worship the Peacock Angel, who pray toward the sun. They came because we refused to be like them.
israel_connection: Israel accepted Yazidi refugees and formally recognized the Yazidi genocide while Arab League states were silent.

resources.label: Nadia Murad — Nobel Peace Prize laureate and survivor testimony

name: Zoroastrian people
subtitle: founders of Persian civilization
note_on_numbers: ~60,000 Parsis in India (descendants of medieval refugees); ~30,000 in diaspora USA/UK/Canada.
native_language: Avestan (liturgical, extinct as spoken), Dari/Middle Persian (historical), modern Persian
native_script: Avestan script (liturgical); historically Pahlavi script; today use Persian script in Iran or Latin in diaspora
arabization_status: Complete Persianate → Arabized transition post-651 CE; Nowruz and cultural traditions survived but Arabized vocabulary dominates modern Persian
language_vitality: Avestan: extinct as spoken language (liturgical only). Zoroastrian community languages: endangered.
human_scale_fact: The Cyrus Cylinder (539 BCE) — the first declaration of human rights in recorded history — was authored by a Zoroastrian king. Nowruz (Persian New Year), celebrated by 300 million people worldwide, is a Zoroastrian holiday predating Islam by over a millennium. The religion that gave the world the concepts of heaven and hell, angels, and the cosmic struggle between good and evil now has fewer followers in its homeland than the population of a small American town.
key_quote: Good thoughts, good words, good deeds. Three words 3,500 years old. They may not survive another century in the land that created them.
key_quote_attribution: Zoroastrian creed — Humata, Hukhta, Huvarshta, c.1500 BCE
israel_connection: Zoroastrian pilgrims and scholars are welcome in Israel; no indigenous community but open access — unlike in Iran where converting to Zoroastrianism is punishable by death.

resources.label: Federation of Zoroastrian Associations of North America

name: Mandaean (Gnostic) people
subtitle: the last living Gnostics
native_language: Mandaic (a dialect of Eastern Aramaic)
native_script: Mandaic script — a cursive alphabet derived from ancient Aramaic; one of the oldest continuously used scripts in the world
arabization_status: Complete in civil life; Mandaic language and script survive only in religious texts and diaspora communities
language_vitality: Critically endangered — estimated fewer than 10,000 speakers worldwide; no country where it has official status
human_scale_fact: Mandaean theology requires baptism in flowing water (masbuta) which must be performed in a natural river or stream. As the community scatters to Western cities, their most sacred ritual becomes logistically impossible. Mandaeans are theologically pacifist — forbidden from bearing arms. In post-2003 Iraq, this made them uniquely defenseless. The largest Mandaean community in the world is now in Sydney, Australia.
key_quote: We cannot convert others. We cannot marry outside our faith. We cannot replace those we lose. Each person who dies or is taken is a door that closes forever.
israel_connection: Small Mandaean community in Israel; able to practice river baptism in the Jordan River and other waterways — a ritual that becomes impossible in many of their diaspora cities.

name: Bahá'í people
subtitle: persecuted in their birthplace, headquartered in Israel
note_on_numbers: Stable in numbers but under severe apartheid-like conditions in Iran; global community 5–8 million.
native_language: Persian (Farsi) — faith founded in Persia
native_script: Persian script; Bahá'í writings in Persian and Arabic
arabization_status: N/A — faith founded in Persian context; faces Islamization not Arabization
language_vitality: Persian: healthy as national language of Iran; Bahá'í specifically not a language community
human_scale_fact: Iran's constitution explicitly protects Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians as religious minorities. It does not mention Bahá'ís — leaving 300,000 people entirely outside legal protection. In response to the university ban, the community created the BIHE (Bahá'í Institute for Higher Education) — an underground university operating since 1987, with professors periodically arrested mid-semester.
key_quote: They can take our buildings, our cemeteries, our jobs, our universities. They cannot take what we know to be true. We have been tested this way for 180 years.
israel_connection: The Bahá'í World Centre — global spiritual and administrative headquarters — sits on Mount Carmel in Haifa; a UNESCO World Heritage Site explicitly chosen by Bahá'u'lláh. Iran executes Bahá'ís while their faith governs itself from the country Iran calls its enemy.

resources.label: Iran Press Watch — Bahá'í persecution documentation
BIHE — Bahá'í Institute for Higher Education

name: Hindus & Sikhs of Afghanistan
subtitle: 3,500 years. Ended in a generation.
native_language: Dari (Afghan Persian), Pashto, Punjabi (Sikhs), Hindi
native_script: Gurmukhi (Sikhs), Devanagari (Hindus), Dari/Persian script for daily life
arabization_status: Complete Islamization — Gandharan place names replaced; Sanskrit inscriptions destroyed; gurdwaras and temples demolished or converted; Hindu/Sikh names forbidden under Taliban
language_vitality: Dari and Pashto: healthy as Afghan national languages but stripped of Hindu/Sikh cultural content; Punjabi in diaspora: vulnerable
human_scale_fact: From 220,000 people in 1992 to 27 in 2023 is a 99.99% decline in 31 years. There is no modern parallel for this speed and completeness of a community's erasure from a country. The Taliban yellow-badge decree for Hindus was explicitly compared by human rights organizations to the Nazi requirement that Jews wear yellow Stars of David.
key_quote: My grandfather's grandfather was born in Kabul. His grandfather before him. We go back so far we have no memory of arriving — only of being here. Now there is no one left to remember that we were ever here at all.
israel_connection: No direct community in Israel; Afghan Hindu/Sikh diaspora is primarily in India, UK, and Canada.

resources.label: Human Rights Watch — Afghanistan religious minorities

name: Kurdish people
subtitle: 40 million people — the largest ethnic group in the world without a state
note_on_numbers: Population not declining but rights, language, and land under continuous attack across all four host states.
native_language: Kurmanji (Northern Kurdish), Sorani (Central Kurdish), Zazaki, Gorani
native_script: Modified Latin (Turkey, diaspora); Arabic-based (Iraq, Iran, Syria); Kurdish Latin alphabet standardized in 1932
arabization_status: Severe in Syria (citizenship stripped 1962; Arabic names imposed; Kurdish schools banned) and Iraq (Saddam's Arabization of Kirkuk). Turkification in Turkey. Persianization in Iran.
language_vitality: Kurmanji: vulnerable (15+ million speakers). Sorani: vulnerable (7+ million speakers). Zazaki: endangered. Gorani: critically endangered.
human_scale_fact: The Halabja chemical attack on March 16, 1988 killed 5,000 Kurdish civilians in a single day — the largest chemical weapons attack against a civilian population in history. Saddam Hussein used nerve agents and mustard gas supplied in part by Western companies. The perpetrators were not prosecuted until 2007. Kurdish women fighters (YPJ) were among the primary forces that defeated ISIS on the ground — widely photographed worldwide, rarely given political recognition.
key_quote: They took our language first. Then our names. Then our villages. The map doesn't show Kurdistan. But we are still here.
israel_connection: Israel has historically maintained diplomatic and intelligence relations with Iraqi Kurds since the 1960s and supported Kurdish autonomy. A small Kurdish Jewish community (Mizrahi) lives in Israel.

name: Baloch people
subtitle: sitting on Pakistan's oil wealth, receiving none of it
note_on_numbers: Population not declining but subjected to enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings, and cultural suppression.
native_language: Balochi (Western, Eastern, Southern dialects)
native_script: Arabic-based Balochi script (Nastaliq style); also written in Latin in diaspora
arabization_status: Severe Urduization in Pakistan — Balochi banned from courts, government, and education; resources extracted by Punjabi-dominated federal government without consent or compensation
language_vitality: Endangered — no official status in any country; excluded from education systems in Pakistan and Iran
human_scale_fact: Balochistan is Pakistan's largest province — 44% of total land area — but contains only 5% of the population, largely due to underdevelopment. The province produces 36% of Pakistan's natural gas and holds vast copper and gold reserves. Baloch communities receive almost no royalties or development. Mothers of the disappeared march in Quetta carrying photographs of their sons — a scene documented by Human Rights Watch for two decades.
key_quote: They take our sons in the night. They return them in plastic bags, weeks later, with their fingernails pulled out. And the world calls this a counterterrorism operation.
key_quote_attribution: Voice of Baloch Missing Persons, Quetta, 2019
israel_connection: No direct connection; some Baloch diaspora activists have sought Israeli recognition of their situation given Iran as a common adversary.

name: Amazigh (Berber) people
subtitle: the indigenous people of North Africa — before the Arabs arrived
note_on_numbers: Population intact but identity, language, and culture systematically suppressed across the Maghreb for decades.
native_language: Tamazight (umbrella term); major dialects: Tachelhit, Tarifit (Rif), Kabyle, Tamasheq (Tuareg), Tachawit
native_script: Tifinagh — one of the oldest scripts in the world; used by Tuareg continuously; recently revived across Maghreb
arabization_status: Systematic Arabization since independence across all Maghrebi states — Amazigh excluded from schools, courts, media, and government until very recently; Gaddafi banned all Berber cultural expression in Libya for 42 years
language_vitality: Kabyle: vulnerable. Tachelhit: vulnerable. Tarifit: endangered. Tamasheq: endangered. Tachawit: critically endangered.
human_scale_fact: The Amazigh people were in North Africa for at least 10,000 years before the Arab conquest of 647 CE. Gaddafi banned Amazigh names so completely that Libyan Berbers gave their children Arabic names publicly and Berber names secretly at home for 42 years. When Gaddafi fell in 2011, elderly Amazigh wept on camera — the first time in their lives they could speak their language in the street.
key_quote: They told us we were Arabs. They changed our names, our street signs, our history books. But you cannot change what a grandmother whispers to her grandchild in the dark.
israel_connection: A small Amazigh-Jewish community (descendants of Berber Jews who converted centuries ago) exists in Israel. Amazigh-Israeli cultural exchange has grown; some Amazigh activists explicitly support normalization with Israel.

name: Nubian people
subtitle: flooded out of their homeland without consent
note_on_numbers: Population grew to 3 million in diaspora, but 100,000 were directly displaced from their ancestral homeland — now submerged under Lake Nasser.
native_language: Nobiin, Kenzi-Dongolawi, Midob (Nile Nubian languages)
native_script: Historically Meroitic script (extinct); Old Nubian (Coptic-based, liturgical); today uses Arabic script
arabization_status: Complete — Nubian languages excluded from all Egyptian education and public life; Nubian place names replaced with Arabic; the Nubian homeland itself no longer exists (submerged)
language_vitality: Nobiin: endangered (500,000 speakers). Kenzi-Dongolawi: endangered. Meroitic: extinct.
human_scale_fact: Nubia was a civilization older than Egypt — with its own pyramids, its own pharaohs (the 25th Dynasty, Nubian kings ruled all of Egypt 744–656 BCE), and its own script (Meroitic, still partially undeciphered). In 1964, Nasser flooded all of it — 500 km of the Nile Valley, 44 villages — to build the Aswan High Dam. Egypt's constitution promises their return to the Nile. Egypt's government arrests them when they ask for it.
key_quote: My grandmother used to describe her house. The color of the door. The tree in the courtyard. The sound of the Nile at night. All of it is under water now. She never stopped describing it.
israel_connection: No direct community in Israel; Nubian issues are largely outside Israeli political context.

name: Alawite civilians
subtitle: a minority at existential risk — distinct from the Assad regime
note_on_numbers: IMPORTANT: Alawite civilians are a religious minority at serious risk. The Assad family is Alawite. The Assad regime committed severe atrocities. These are separate facts. The crimes of a regime do not justify collective punishment of a community.
native_language: Arabic (Syrian dialect)
native_script: Arabic script — fully Arabized
arabization_status: Alawites are Arab-speaking; their distinctiveness is religious not linguistic; Alawite religious texts (partly secret) maintained in Arabic
language_vitality: N/A — Arabic is native language
human_scale_fact: Alawites practice a syncretic faith incorporating elements of Shia Islam, Christianity (they celebrate Christmas and Easter), and ancient pre-Islamic Syrian religion. They were historically the poorest and most marginalized community in French Mandate Syria — the French deliberately recruited them into the military as a counterweight to Sunni Arab nationalism. The Assad family's rise to power used Alawite military positioning as its base — and now ordinary Alawite farmers and fishermen on the Syrian coast face being killed in their name.
key_quote: I never voted for Assad. My family never wanted this war. We are farmers. We are fishermen. But now they come to our villages and they kill us for his crimes.
israel_connection: Small Alawite community on the Golan Heights; their situation is complex given Israeli-Syrian border dynamics.

resources.label: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria

name: Circassian people
subtitle: survivors of Russia's forgotten genocide of 1864
note_on_numbers: Global Circassian diaspora 3–7 million (estimates vary widely); 700,000 is the figure for MENA countries specifically.
native_language: Adyghe (West Circassian), Kabardian (East Circassian) — Northwest Caucasian language family
native_script: Cyrillic script (imposed in Soviet era); no classical Circassian script survived
arabization_status: Significant — Circassians in Arab countries adopted Arabic for public life; language maintained in home and community but not transmitted to all younger generations
language_vitality: Adyghe: endangered (500,000 speakers). Kabardian: vulnerable (600,000 speakers). Both critically endangered outside Russia.
human_scale_fact: The 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics were held on the exact site where, 150 years earlier, the final Circassian deportations took place — the beach from which hundreds of thousands of Circassians were loaded onto boats, many of which sank. Russia has never recognized the Circassian genocide. The Circassians in Jordan and Israel have maintained their language and identity better than those in Turkey, where 200 years of assimilation pressure has reduced many to 'Turks who dance Circassian dances at weddings.'
key_quote: On the Day of Mourning we do not celebrate. We remember 1864. We remember the boats. We remember the beach at Sochi that the Olympics tried to make us forget.
israel_connection: ~4,000–5,000 Circassians are full Israeli citizens in Kfar Kama and Rehaniya; male Circassians serve in the IDF by community request since 1958 — one of the best-preserved Circassian communities outside Russia.

name: Ahwazi Arab people
subtitle: Arabic speakers in Iran — sitting on 80% of Iran's oil
native_language: Arabic (Khuzestani dialect)
native_script: Arabic script — same as official Iranian Arabic; but Arabic education is banned in Iranian schools
arabization_status: Inverse — Ahwazis are Arab speakers facing Persianization; Arabic language banned from schools in Khuzestan; Persian names imposed on Arab towns and streets
language_vitality: Khuzestani Arabic: endangered in Iran due to institutional suppression; children educated only in Persian
human_scale_fact: Khuzestan Province — the Ahwazi homeland — produces approximately 80% of Iran's oil and 60% of its gas. The Ahwazi Arab population lives in poverty while their land's resources fund the Iranian state. They cannot attend school in their own language. The rivers of their province are diverted to Persian-majority regions. In 2021, people were photographed drinking from muddy puddles in one of the world's most oil-rich regions.
key_quote: They tell us we are Iranian. But they teach our children in Persian. They take our water. They take our oil. They give us nothing. And then they arrest us for saying so.
key_quote_attribution: Ahwazi Arab activist, in exile, London, 2021
israel_connection: Ahwazi Arab activists have sometimes sought Israeli media coverage and political attention given Iran as a common adversary — a complex political dynamic.

name: Dom people (Middle Eastern Roma)
subtitle: stateless, undocumented, invisible
note_on_numbers: Estimated — no census anywhere counts Dom population; extreme undercounting likely.
native_language: Domari (Indo-Aryan language, related to Romani) — also called 'the language of Dom'
native_script: No classical script; Domari increasingly written in Arabic script; critically endangered
arabization_status: Complete in public life; Domari suppressed by association with poverty and marginalization; many Dom hide their identity and speak only Arabic publicly
language_vitality: Critically endangered — estimated 500,000 speakers remaining; UNESCO lists as 'definitely endangered'
human_scale_fact: The Dom are the 'other Roma' — the branch of the original Indian diaspora that migrated west through Persia and settled in the Middle East, while the European Roma continued into the Balkans. In Lebanon, Dom children are frequently denied birth registration — making them stateless in the most literal sense: they do not legally exist. They cannot attend school, access healthcare, or cross borders.
key_quote: We have no country. We have no papers. We have no rights. We have only our music. And in some places, they have taken that too.
israel_connection: Small Dom community in Israel; some receive citizenship and legal status — a relatively better situation than in most Arab states.

resources.label: Domari Society of Gypsies in Jerusalem
Minority Rights Group — Dom in the Middle East

name: Shia Muslims
subtitle: persecuted as heretics by co-religionists
note_on_numbers: ~15% of all Muslims globally; majority in Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain; large minorities in Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Lebanon, Kuwait.
native_language: Arabic, Persian, Urdu — no distinct Shia language
native_script: Arabic script — same as Sunni communities
arabization_status: N/A — Shia are Arabic speakers in the Arab world; suppression is religious, not linguistic
language_vitality: N/A
human_scale_fact: In Bahrain, Shia Muslims are 65–70% of the citizen population — a clear majority — yet are systematically excluded from the military, security services, and senior government positions by a Sunni monarchy backed by Saudi Arabia and the United States. In 2011, Bahraini Shia rose in peaceful protest during the Arab Spring; Saudi Arabia sent troops to suppress them. In Pakistan, Shia doctors, lawyers, and academics are targeted on 'kill lists' — their names and professions circulated in leaflets, their murders carried out in broad daylight.
key_quote: We say the same shahada. We face the same Mecca. We fast the same Ramadan. And they say we are not Muslim. And then they kill us.
israel_connection: Iran is the primary Shia theocracy and state sponsor of anti-Israel activity; Iraqi and Lebanese Shia militias armed by Iran. Complex relationship — Shia civilians are often caught between Iranian regime ambitions and their own interests.

resources.label: Human Rights Watch — Hazara Shia Pakistan
Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy

name: Ahmadi Muslims
subtitle: the only people in the world declared non-Muslim by constitutional amendment
note_on_numbers: Population stable but living under legal persecution; global community ~10 million.
native_language: Urdu, Punjabi, English
native_script: Urdu/Nastaliq script, Latin script
arabization_status: N/A — Ahmadis are South Asian; persecution is religious identity suppression, not Arabization
language_vitality: N/A
human_scale_fact: Pakistan is the only country in the world that has legally defined a religious group as non-Muslim by constitutional amendment. Ahmadi graves in Pakistan are regularly vandalized; epitaphs quoting the Quran must be removed or the family faces prosecution. In Indonesia, Ahmadis have been banned from preaching since 2008; dozens of mosques destroyed by mobs with police standing by. The Ahmadiyya mosque in Haifa, Israel has operated legally since 1928.
key_quote: I cannot say Assalamu Alaikum in my own country. This greeting — the greeting of peace — is illegal for me to use. Because of who I am.
israel_connection: The Ahmadiyya national headquarters and mosque in Kababir neighborhood, Haifa has operated legally since 1928. The community can call their worship site a mosque freely — a stark contrast with Pakistan where this is a criminal act.

resources.label: Rabwah Times — Ahmadi news and persecution documentation
US Commission on International Religious Freedom — Pakistan

name: Alevi Muslims
subtitle: 15–20 million people — the largest religious minority in any Muslim country, invisible to their own state
note_on_numbers: Population stable but facing structural state discrimination; ~700,000 in German diaspora.
native_language: Turkish, Kurdish (Zazaki, Kurmanji) — Alevis are multiethnic
native_script: Latin (Turkey, post-1928); no distinct Alevi script
arabization_status: N/A — Turkey is not Arab; Alevis face Sunnification/Turkification; Ottoman-era suppression of Alevi practices was systematic
language_vitality: Zazaki (Kurdish dialect spoken by many Alevis): endangered. Turkish: healthy. Alevi Dede oral poetry tradition: at risk.
human_scale_fact: Turkey's Directorate of Religious Affairs (Diyanet) employs 80,000 Sunni imams, funds thousands of mosques, and is paid for by all Turkish taxpayers — including 15–20 million Alevis. The Diyanet does not recognize Alevi religious practice. Alevi children in Turkish state schools are required to take Sunni Islamic religious education classes — the European Court of Human Rights has ruled this violates religious freedom multiple times; Turkey has not complied.
key_quote: We are told we are Muslim. But our Islam has no mosque, no veil, no separation of men and women. We light candles, we play the saz, we weep for Karbala. And for this, they have always come to kill us.
israel_connection: Some Alevi diaspora in Germany have expressed solidarity with Israel; complex political alignment given Turkish government hostility to Israel under AKP.

name: Ismaili Muslims
subtitle: founded Al-Azhar. Now considered heretics by its faculty.
note_on_numbers: Population stable globally; targeted in specific regions (Pakistan, Afghanistan, Tajikistan).
native_language: Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Tajik, various local languages
native_script: Arabic/Persian scripts; Burushaski and other Pamir languages also spoken
arabization_status: N/A — Ismailis span Arab and non-Arab contexts; face Sunnification not Arabization
language_vitality: N/A as a distinct Ismaili language; Burushaski (spoken by some Ismailis in Pakistan): endangered
human_scale_fact: Al-Azhar University in Cairo — the most prestigious institution in Sunni Islam, whose fatwas are followed by millions — was founded in 970 CE by the Fatimid Ismaili Caliphate. Its founders would be considered heretics by its current faculty. The Aga Khan Development Network operates in 30+ countries and invests approximately $800 million annually in health, education, and poverty reduction, primarily in Muslim-majority countries.
key_quote: We are told our Imam is heresy. That our women who go to school are shameless. We have heard this for 1,200 years. We are still here.
israel_connection: No direct community; the Aga Khan Development Network operates in some contexts adjacent to Israeli humanitarian initiatives.

name: Sufi Muslims & shrine culture
subtitle: the dominant form of popular Islam for 1,000 years — now being demolished
note_on_numbers: Sufism is a practice within Islam, not a discrete population; shrine pilgrimage involves hundreds of millions; distinct Sufi orders: millions of initiated members.
native_language: Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Turkish — Sufism crosses language communities
native_script: Arabic, Persian scripts; Sufi poetry in Ottoman Turkish; Hausa (West Africa)
arabization_status: Wahhabi-funded Arabization of Islamic practice is destroying Sufi shrine culture — replacing local syncretic saint veneration with Gulf-exported puritanism
language_vitality: Sufi musical traditions (qawwali, sama, hadra) endangered by religious prohibition; Sufi poetry in endangered languages at risk
human_scale_fact: Saudi Arabia demolished over 400 historical Islamic sites in Mecca and Medina between 1985 and 2015 — including buildings from the time of the Prophet — to build hotels and parking lots. The ICC prosecution of Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi for destroying Timbuktu's shrines was the first time the destruction of cultural heritage was prosecuted as a war crime in its own right.
key_quote: They say our music is haram. Our dancing is haram. Our love for the saints is shirk. They came and they bombed us while we were praying. While we were singing to God.
key_quote_attribution: Survivor, Sehwan Sharif shrine bombing, Pakistan, 2017
israel_connection: No direct connection; some Sufi orders were historically present in Ottoman Palestine; limited contemporary relationship.

resources.label: Pakistan Institute for Peace Studies — shrine attacks

name: Sexual & gender minorities
subtitle: the one minority that cuts across every other group on this list
note_on_numbers: No reliable population data — criminalization prevents self-identification; estimated 5–10% of any population applies regionally.
native_language: N/A — cross-cutting identity
native_script: N/A
arabization_status: Notable: classical Arabic literature (Abbasid era), Persian poetry (Hafez, Rumi), and Ottoman court culture all contain extensive homoerotic literary traditions. The criminalization of same-sex relations is largely a 19th-century British colonial legal legacy (Section 377) and 20th-century Islamist movement, not ancient tradition.
language_vitality: N/A
human_scale_fact: Iran executes gay men by hanging — estimated 4,000–6,000 since the Islamic Revolution. Israel, by contrast, grants asylum to gay Palestinians, Egyptians, Iranians, and Syrians fleeing persecution. Tel Aviv has hosted Pride since 1993. The classical Persian poet Hafez wrote extensively of male love. The criminalization of homosexuality in much of the region is not ancient tradition — it is largely a product of British colonialism and 20th-century Islamist politics.
key_quote: I left Iran because they would have killed me. I came to Israel because here I can live as I am. My family thinks I am in Germany. They cannot know where I really am.
key_quote_attribution: Iranian gay asylum seeker, Tel Aviv, 2019
israel_connection: Israel is the only country in the Middle East where same-sex relations are fully legal. Tel Aviv Pride is one of the world's largest. Israel grants asylum to LGBTQ+ individuals from MENA countries. The IDF has no restrictions on LGBTQ+ service members.

name: Buddhist civilization of Central Asia
subtitle: dominant from Afghanistan to Uzbekistan for 1,000 years. Nothing remains.
note_on_numbers: No indigenous Buddhist community anywhere in MENA or Central Asia; this entry documents a civilization, not a living community.
native_language: Gandhari Prakrit, Sanskrit, Sogdian, Bactrian, Tocharian
native_script: Kharosthi (indigenous to Gandhara — invented in the region, now extinct); Brahmi; Sogdian; Bactrian Greek
arabization_status: Total and complete — every place name, institutional name, cultural marker, and script was replaced; Kharosthi script extinct
language_vitality: Gandhari Prakrit: extinct. Sogdian: extinct. Bactrian: extinct. Kharosthi script: extinct.
human_scale_fact: The larger Bamiyan Buddha (Salsal, 55 meters) was carved in 554 CE. The Taliban spent 25 days in March 2001 destroying it using dynamite, anti-aircraft guns, and artillery, despite appeals from UNESCO and the UN Secretary-General. The Gandharan Buddhist art style — created in modern Pakistan and Afghanistan — fused Indian Buddhist iconography with Greek artistic technique from Alexander the Great's campaigns. It is the origin of the iconic image of the meditating Buddha that spread to China, Japan, Korea, and Southeast Asia.
key_quote: When they blew up the Buddhas, they did not destroy stone. They destroyed the proof that this place was once a meeting point of civilizations. That is what they wanted to erase.
israel_connection: Israeli archaeologists and scholars have documented Gandharan art and Central Asian Buddhist history; no direct community connection.
